baseline_models.focus_anchor: أقتل موسى ... أخاف أن يبدل دينكم أو أن يظهر في الأرض الفساد
baseline_models.mechanism: Pharaoh converts a proposed killing into preventive policy: remove the person before either replacement of the community's governing allegiance or the public emergence and prevalence of disorder.

activation_trace.role: Literal taking of life supplies the coercive intervention presented as prevention.
Expectation of a marked harm supplies the anticipatory logic for acting before evidence matures.
One thing standing in another's place makes replacement, not mere criticism, the first alleged danger.
Obedience and submission make din the community's practiced allegiance as well as its creed.
Rising into dominance gives the second danger a political sense of disorder becoming prevalent.
Departure from soundness supplies the adverse condition Pharaoh claims to forestall.

changed_reading.before: Pharaoh simply threatens to kill Moses.
changed_reading.after: Pharaoh frames lethal removal as anticipatory state protection against a transfer of allegiance or the public dominance of disorder.

baseline_models.mechanism: The possessives set rival jurisdictions against each other: Moses has a Lord, while the audience has a din whose branches include obedience, domination, customary order, and the city organized by authority.

activation_trace.role: Lordship as mastery and sovereignty supplies the rival authority named as Moses's.
Substitution makes the feared event a transfer from one authority relation to another.
Subjugation and rule expose the coercive political dimension inside 'your din.'
Habit and established practice make the threatened object a lived social order.
The city of obedience gives the possessive din a civic and institutional scope.

changed_reading.before: Moses might change the people's religious beliefs.
changed_reading.after: Moses threatens to transfer obedience and public jurisdiction away from Pharaoh's civic-religious order toward another Lord.

baseline_models.mechanism: The clause can carry two live directions: Moses may make disorder prevail, but he may also make an already present failure visible on the land's public surface. Pharaoh's wording does not identify whether Moses originates or exposes it.

activation_trace.role: Emergence and disclosure supply the possibility that the act is revelation rather than production.
Ascendancy and prevalence preserve the competing reading that disorder is made dominant.
The terrestrial domain supplies the public field in which either disclosure or prevalence occurs.
Loss of soundness names the condition whose source Pharaoh leaves strategically unspecified.

changed_reading.before: Moses will introduce corruption into the land.
changed_reading.after: Pharaoh alleges either that Moses will make disorder dominant or that he will bring a corrupt condition into public visibility; the causation remains rhetorically underdetermined.

baseline_models.mechanism: Two permissive imperatives stage an efficacy contest: others are told to release Pharaoh toward killing, while Moses is released toward calling. The first action claims bodily reach; the second invokes rival lordship.

activation_trace.role: Leaving or releasing supplies the permission frame around Pharaoh's proposed action.
Lethal efficacy is Pharaoh's side of the staged contest.
Calling and drawing by speech supply Moses's counter-action.
Sovereign mastery identifies the power whose response Pharaoh implicitly challenges.
The effective speech of a ruler frames the whole scene as an attempted performative decree.

changed_reading.before: Pharaoh dismissively permits Moses to pray while threatening him.
changed_reading.after: Pharaoh scripts a public test between his own permission-dependent power to kill and Moses's call to a rival sovereign.

context_deltas.mechanism: Earlier context supplies a repeated sequence in which communities form an intention against a messenger, seize him, and twist argument in order to dislodge truth; the immediately preceding ayah supplies an actual killing policy. Pharaoh's preventive rationale now reads as the local wording of a recurrent coercive script.

activation_trace.role: The proposed taking of Moses's life anchors the recurring coercive mechanism in the focus.
An intention congealed within the self supplies the pre-action stage of the messenger-seizure pattern.
Capture and confinement connect the nations' attempted seizure of messengers with the answering seizure of the aggressors.
Twisted disputation supplies the rhetorical wrapping placed around coercion.
The attempted collapse of a proof supplies the declared argumentative aim behind seizure.
The preceding command to kill believers' sons makes lethal policy actual before Pharaoh individualizes it against Moses.

structural_cues: 40:5 orders intention, messenger-seizure, twisted dispute, attempted displacement of truth, and counter-seizure.
40:25 places an enacted collective killing command immediately before the focus's singular proposal.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies the repeated sequence and the adjacent killing command; I infer that Pharaoh's announced fear rationalizes his place in that sequence. A materially live alternative is that he also experiences genuine political fear while reproducing the pattern.

changed_reading.before: The killing is an exceptional response to a new security threat.
changed_reading.after: The speech is a familiar messenger-seizure script in which preventive language and argumentative displacement prepare coercion.

context_deltas.mechanism: Moses immediately performs the supposedly permitted call as asylum in 'my Lord and your Lord,' undoing Pharaoh's possessive distancing. A concealed believer then states the present charge directly: killing a man for saying 'my Lord is God.' The feared future disruption is revised into hostility toward an already spoken transfer of lordship.

activation_trace.role: The permitted call anchors the response that the next ayah performs.
Moses's apparently private sovereign is the relation the context universalizes.
Seeking refuge and attachment turns calling into an effective jurisdictional appeal.
Mastery shared by 'my' and 'your' Lord breaks Pharaoh's attempt to isolate Moses's patron.
The day of account supplies the superior jurisdiction denied by the arrogant threat.
Concealment of faith creates an internal witness whose disclosure counters Pharaoh's public rationale.
The believer repeats literal killing as the act that needs justification.
Speech as professed belief identifies the utterance of lordship as the immediate ground of persecution.

structural_cues: 40:27 directly follows Pharaoh's 'let him call' with Moses's first-person refuge formula.
40:28 converts Pharaoh's projected future harms into the believer's present causal question: killing because a man says who his Lord is.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies the immediate call, the pronoun expansion, and the believer's causal challenge; I infer that these expose allegiance as the operative charge. An alternative is that the believer strategically narrows a genuinely broader security case.

changed_reading.before: Moses may appeal to a private Lord after Pharaoh acts for public safety.
changed_reading.after: Moses invokes the Lord of both parties as a higher asylum, and the next speaker exposes confession of that lordship as the present reason for the threatened killing.

context_deltas.mechanism: The believing man repeats Pharaoh's exact posture of fearing 'for you,' but grounds it in patterned historical consequences and the day of mutual calling. Fear becomes a contested claim to protective care rather than transparent evidence of motive.

activation_trace.role: Pharaoh's expectation of harm anchors the first protective claim.
The believer reuses anticipated harm to make a rival claim of concern for the same audience.
An exemplary warning gives the believer's fear a historical evidentiary mechanism.
A severe event shifts the feared harm from regime change to consequence.
Repetition stabilizes the believer's counter-fear as a sustained protective stance.
Raised calling makes the feared day a public field of answering voices, countering Pharaoh's control of who may call.

structural_cues: 40:30 and 40:32 repeat the focus's first-person fear construction in the mouth of the concealed believer.
The believer's fear points backward to repeated peoples and forward to judgment, whereas Pharaoh's points toward suppressing Moses.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies parallel fear speeches with different objects and remedies; I infer that the parallel invites evaluation of fear by its causal warrant and proposed action. Both speakers could still be sincere at the affective level.

changed_reading.before: Pharaoh's fear straightforwardly authenticates his concern for the people.
changed_reading.after: Fear is rival political-pastoral rhetoric: Pharaoh's fear authorizes killing, while the believer's fear authorizes warning through historical analogy.

context_deltas.mechanism: Whole-surah visibility repeatedly moves from concealed interiors to compulsory exposure. The court itself is described as dominant in the land, Pharaoh claims exclusive control of what he shows, and pride is located in breasts. The focus's 'make corruption appear' can therefore expose the dominant regime's hidden source of action even while retaining the reading 'make corruption prevail.'

activation_trace.role: Disclosure anchors the possibility that Moses makes a concealed condition publicly legible.
Loss of soundness is the condition whose true location is reopened by the context.
Universal emergence into exposure establishes the surah's terminal visibility horizon.
Hidden content supplies the interior counterpart to what the focus says may be made visible.
The breast as the source from which acts issue relocates causation beneath public claims.
Concealed faith demonstrates that the court's visible consensus contains a hidden counter-position.
The court's current dominance in the land activates the political-prevalence branch of the focus verb.
Pharaoh's claim that he only shows what he sees makes visibility itself an instrument of rule.
Pride magnified within the breast supplies a concealed motive beneath public disputation.

structural_cues: 40:16 and 40:19 pair total exposure with knowledge of concealed interiors.
40:29 places the same ظهر root in 'dominant in the land' and follows it with Pharaoh's monopoly claim over showing and seeing.
40:28 and 40:56 locate opposed hidden contents inside the regime: concealed faith and concealed pride.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies the disclosure lexicon, the regime's visible dominance, and hidden interiors; I infer that Moses's feared act may reveal the regime's own corruption. The alternative that Pharaoh means only the future prevalence of Moses-caused disorder remains fully live.

changed_reading.before: The visible danger is corruption generated by Moses outside the regime.
changed_reading.after: Visibility is contested political control: Moses may make disorder prevail, but he may instead expose the hidden corruption of the order already dominant in the land.

context_deltas.mechanism: After daring Moses to call his Lord, Pharaoh orders a high structure, seeks a chain of means to reach and inspect Moses's God, then declares Moses a liar. The verbal challenge becomes an attempted surveillance and containment of rival lordship within Pharaoh's own vertical apparatus.

activation_trace.role: Moses's call anchors the rival relation Pharaoh later tries to inspect.
The called sovereign is converted by Pharaoh into an alleged object at the end of a built route.
A high construction supplies the material instrument of Pharaoh's counter-inquiry.
Reaching an endpoint supplies the assumed arrow from architecture to access.
A rope or connecting means turns the heavens into a traversable chain in Pharaoh's model.
Overlooking and uncovering an affair supply the surveillance goal.
Uncertain supposition reveals that the inquiry begins from a conclusion it claims to verify.
Loss and ruin mark the failure of the apparatus that sought to contain the call.

structural_cues: 40:36-37 follows the focus with a command to build, a vertical reach, an attempted look toward Moses's God, and a prior declaration of falsehood.
The same speaker who permits the call then tries to make its addressee available to his own visual regime.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies the call, tower, chain of means, inspection, and declared suspicion; I infer a counter-call mechanism in which Pharaoh tries to domesticate rival lordship through surveillance. The tower may alternatively be pure public spectacle rather than sincere inquiry.

changed_reading.before: Letting Moses call is a disposable taunt.
changed_reading.after: The taunt initiates Pharaoh's failed attempt to bring the called Lord within an architecture of reach, sight, and official verification.

context_deltas.mechanism: Later calls are explicitly directional: the believer calls toward rescue while his people call toward fire, then entrusts his affair to God. God finally commands 'call Me' and supplies the missing response, while refusal is tied to pride against service. Pharaoh's challenge to Moses's call is answered by a surah-wide invitation-response system.

activation_trace.role: The focus call anchors the efficacy question later calls resolve.
The challenged Lord is the speaker who later invites and answers calling.
Opposed vocal invitations supply two destinations and make calling socially directional.
Rescue as separation supplies the destination of the believer's counter-call.
Entrusting the affair to another supplies the operational completion of appeal to higher authority.
The direct invitation to call removes Pharaoh's assumed control over whether the appeal may occur.
Answering speech supplies the explicit efficacy that Pharaoh's dare leaves in question.
Submissive service joins call-response to the allegiance contested in 'your din.'

structural_cues: 40:41-44 develops repeated calls with opposed destinations and ends in entrusting the affair to God.
40:60 places call and answer in immediate verbal sequence, then identifies pride against service as the refusal mechanism.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies opposed calls, entrustment, and an explicit divine answer; I infer that these retrospectively answer Pharaoh's efficacy challenge. The focus may still portray Pharaoh as merely contemptuous rather than consciously testing a response.

changed_reading.before: Moses's call is an impotent accompaniment to Pharaoh's lethal action.
changed_reading.after: Calling is the surah's directional and responsive mechanism: it moves people toward rival ends, transfers an affair, and receives an answer from the Lord Pharaoh challenges.

context_deltas.mechanism: Pharaoh says of Moses, 'let him call his Lord.' Later those in the fire ask the keepers, 'call your Lord' to reduce one day of punishment, and are told to call for themselves, but their call is lost. The same possessive distancing and delegated appeal return against Pharaoh's side.

activation_trace.role: The third-person appeal supplies the wording later mirrored by the condemned speakers.
The distancing possessive 'his Lord' anchors the reversal to 'your Lord.'
A delegated call repeats Pharaoh's grammar from the position of need.
Calling the keepers' master 'your Lord' preserves the earlier refusal to own the relation.
Reduction in amount supplies the minimal relief now sought from the once-dismissed authority.
The command to call and the failed calling of disbelievers complete the reversal.
Loss makes the late delegated call fail to arrive at the relief it seeks.

structural_cues: 40:49 reproduces the focus's call-plus-possessive-Lord construction with changed pronouns and reversed power.
40:50 answers the delegation by returning the imperative to the speakers and declaring the disbelievers' call lost.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies the close grammatical mirror and its failed outcome; I infer deliberate temporal reversal of Pharaoh's dare. The later speakers are a broader condemned collective, so identification with Pharaoh's immediate court remains narrative rather than one-to-one.

changed_reading.before: Pharaoh can distance himself from Moses's Lord and leave Moses alone to call.
changed_reading.after: That distancing grammar returns from the position of helplessness: Pharaoh's side delegates a call to another's Lord and discovers that the refused relation cannot be outsourced at the end.

context_deltas.mechanism: The surah brackets Pharaoh's 'your din' with commands to make din exclusive for God, narrates guidance and the Book passing by inheritance to Israel, and commands submission to the Lord of the worlds. Din is removed from Pharaoh's possessive custody and recast as exclusive allegiance that can outlive coercion through transmitted guidance.

activation_trace.role: Replacement anchors Pharaoh's fear that one normative order will stand where another stood.
Obedience and worship supply the relation being reassigned.
Exclusive separation from association removes din from mixed or partisan ownership.
Din as obedient worship is explicitly directed to God before Pharaoh calls it 'yours.'
Transmission of knowledge or Book by inheritance supplies a noncoercive mechanism of normative succession.
Gentle guidance toward the right path names what survives Pharaoh's attempted suppression.
A written fixing that establishes judgment gives inherited guidance durable normative form.
The repeated exclusive din confirms that allegiance is God's rather than a ruler's possession.
Handing oneself over supplies the enacted posture toward the Lord of the worlds.

structural_cues: 40:14 precedes the focus with din made exclusive for God; 40:65 repeats the formula after the Pharaoh narrative.
40:53 places Moses, guidance, Israelite inheritance, and the Book in one succession statement.
40:66 opposes worship of what the audience calls to submission to the Lord of all worlds.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies exclusive din, inherited guidance, and commanded submission; I infer that these de-possess Pharaoh's 'your din' and narrate the feared change as durable succession. The inheritance verse need not denote a direct administrative replacement of Egypt's order.

changed_reading.before: Pharaoh protects a community-owned religion from unauthorized alteration.
changed_reading.after: His possessive formula tries to hold allegiance in place, while the surah assigns din exclusively to God and shows guidance surviving as inherited written order.

context_deltas.mechanism: Pharaoh's royal speech proposes death but first asks others to release him and later fails. Divine speech gives life and death, issues a decisive affair, says 'be,' and the event occurs; messengers themselves bring signs only by divine permission. The efficacy contest is resolved by relocating command, authorization, and realization.

activation_trace.role: The ruler's consequential speech anchors the attempted human decree.
The request to be released reveals that Pharaoh's action remains socially mediated.
Taking life is the efficacy Pharaoh claims for his speech.
Removing life places the power Pharaoh claims within the divine subject's scope.
A decisive judgment or command supplies finality without Pharaoh's deliberative permission scene.
Binding command identifies the affair whose realization follows speech.
Uttered saying supplies the verbal act immediately paired with realization.
Occurrence and presence in time supply the event that answers the command without delay.
Authorization limits even a messenger's sign to divine permission, clarifying the hierarchy of effective agency.

structural_cues: The focus sequences Pharaoh's saying, request for release, intended killing, and Moses's call.
40:68 compresses divine life, death, decision, saying, and occurrence into one causal sequence.
40:78 explicitly places messenger-signs under permission and final judgment under God's command.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies contrasting speech-action sequences and explicit authorization; I infer that the later sequence resolves the focus's sovereignty test. The theological contrast does not erase the real delegated violence available to Pharaoh in the immediate scene.

changed_reading.before: Pharaoh's command controls death, while Moses can only speak upward.
changed_reading.after: Pharaoh's lethal decree is mediated and frustrated; life, death, authorization, decisive command, and self-realizing speech belong to the Lord Moses calls.

surprising_valid_outliers.containment: This is surprising because financial debt is not the ordinary local rendering of din, but it remains anchored in the packet's din branches and is activated by the surah's earned recompense, debt-collection image, and repeated account. Downstream prose should present it as a jurisdictional ledger analogy, not as a replacement translation.

activation_trace.role: Judgment and recompense make din an accountability regime as well as confession.
Financial debt supplies the exploratory ledger image for obligations owed under a ruler.
Collecting and satisfying a debt makes recompense function like settlement of an account.
Acquired earnings supply what is entered on the moral ledger.
Counting and account supply the reckoning that closes the ledger.
Disbelief in the day of account connects Pharaoh's arrogant order to refusal of superior settlement.

changed_reading.before: Moses may replace a set of beliefs.
changed_reading.after: Exploratorily, Pharaoh fears that Moses will change the ledger of obligation: who is obeyed, what is owed, and before whose account actions are finally settled.

surprising_valid_outliers.containment: This is a deliberately cross-domain material analogy built from peripheral earth branches: wood-boring consumption and a suppurating lesion. It remains valid because both branches attach directly to الأرض beside يظهر and الفساد, while the context repeatedly exposes hidden interiors. It should be rendered only as an exploratory image of internal decay, never as the lexical meaning of الأرض.

activation_trace.role: Disclosure supplies the movement from concealed decay to visible condition.
A wood-borer consuming material from within supplies one contained image for latent civic decay.
An ulcer spoiled by collected matter supplies a second image for corruption becoming externally legible.
Departure from soundness is the shared condition linking the material analogy to the focus.
Concealment supplies the hidden phase before exposure.
The interior source from which acts issue makes the body-politic analogy causally coherent.

changed_reading.before: Moses imports an external disorder into an otherwise sound land.
changed_reading.after: As a contained material analogy, Moses may expose corruption already eating or suppurating within the land's political body.

surprising_valid_outliers.containment: The root branch 'complete mastery in knowledge' is form-distant from the unequivocally lethal syntax and cannot displace literal killing, which nearby ayat reinforce. It remains worth carrying because Pharaoh later builds an apparatus to inspect and settle Moses's claim. Downstream prose should treat it as a secondary motive-layer coupling elimination with attempted epistemic capture.

activation_trace.role: Complete epistemic mastery supplies the exploratory sense of settling Moses's claim by conquering it.
The high structure materializes an apparatus for mastering the rival claim.
Reaching the endpoint supplies the assumption that the claim can be exhaustively accessed.
Inspection and uncovering supply the knowledge operation that accompanies coercion.
Supposition and doubt show the unresolved claim Pharaoh seeks to close while already calling it false.

changed_reading.before: Pharaoh seeks only Moses's bodily death.
changed_reading.after: Without weakening the literal threat, the killing proposal also carries an exploratory drive to master, settle, and close Moses's claim through coercive knowledge.

surprising_valid_outliers.containment: This activation uses the packet's non-dominant split mapping from دعو to دعع, so it is intentionally branch-distant. It remains anchored because the focus call is syntactically paired with Pharaoh's force and later calls explicitly direct people toward rescue or fire. Render it only as a force-vector metaphor, never as a lexical substitution for 'call.'

activation_trace.role: A forceful push supplies the exploratory image of the call exerting counter-pressure against Pharaoh's decree.
Lethal force supplies the opposed vector with which the call is paired.
Opposed calls toward rescue and fire make speech function as social propulsion.
Rescue by separation supplies one destination toward which the counter-force moves.
The answering return supplies the reciprocal motion that completes the call.

changed_reading.before: Moses's call is passive speech beside Pharaoh's physical force.
changed_reading.after: As a contained split-root metaphor, the call is a counter-force that redirects allegiance and receives an answering return.

strongest_changes: The alleged future security threat becomes a recurrent messenger-seizure script and is immediately exposed as hostility to a spoken transfer of lordship.
Moses answers 'let him call his Lord' by seeking refuge in 'my Lord and your Lord,' defeating Pharaoh's possessive distancing.
The believer's repeated 'I fear for you' turns fear into a contest between rival claims of protective care.
The visibility clause can turn back on the dominant regime: Moses may expose hidden corruption rather than originate it.
The surah answers Pharaoh's dare with call-and-response, then reverses his grammar when the condemned ask others to 'call your Lord' for them.
Pharaoh's mediated lethal decree is finally contrasted with divine life, death, authorization, decisive command, and self-realizing speech.
summary.what_was_special: The whole-surah packet made one compact speech recur as a network of pronoun reversals, rival fear claims, visibility controls, delegated calls, and competing speech-action systems. The most diagnostic activation was not a new topic but the return of Pharaoh's own wording from positions he could not control.
remaining_uncertainties: The focus verb يظهر still supports both disclosure and political prevalence; context strengthens both rather than disambiguating them.
Pharaoh's fear may be affectively sincere even if the narrative pattern makes it a coercive rationale.
The tower may be a sincere but category-bound inquiry, a public spectacle, or both.
The obligation-ledger, internal-rot, epistemic-capture, and split-root force readings are exploratory analogies and must not replace the dominant lexical senses.
